technique: entering mid-action, with no setup at all
lesson: Today we work on one technique. It is called entering mid-action. That means the poem starts while something is already happening, with no explanation of who, where, or why. This poem does that. It opens with "Cold pine in the shop, that resin smell." No name, no date, no setup. You are already there. A few lines later it says "You stand there breathing it." You still don't know who the person is. Then "There's a small thing finished and set where you'll see it." The poem trusts you to catch up on your own. This works because it makes you pay attention right away. You have to figure out the scene while it moves, so you lean in. Try this: cut your first two sentences of explaining and start on a smell, an object, or an action already in progress. The second time through, listen for how fast you understand the scene without being told. Here is the poem.
poem:
Cold pine in the shop, that resin smell
that gets into the wool of your sleeves and stays,
sawdust gone sweet in the unheated dark
where the stove hasn't caught yet. You stand there
breathing it, the way a man does before he's spoken
to anyone, the hills outside holding their gray
a while longer. There's a small thing finished
and set where you'll see it—a window cut true
into the face of the board, three seasons deep.
You turn it once in the flat early gray,
thumbing the edge of what your own two hands made.

The grain took your mark and held it—
one of one, and the day's not even started.
